name: Antibacterial soap (Hibiclens)

lead: Hibiclens is a hospital-grade antiseptic wash that looksmaxxing posters use on the underarms for fresher-smelling skin.

Chlorhexidine binds bacterial cell walls, stopping growth or killing bacteria depending on concentration. It is used to prepare skin before surgery, clean wounds and in surgical scrubs, and in one US trial daily bathing of ICU patients with chlorhexidine cloths reduced hospital-acquired infections. Studies of it for cosmetic body odor were not found.

paras: Used as a body or underarm wash in the shower, left on briefly and rinsed off, as an occasional step beside the usual routine. Sold over the counter in the US.
Skin irritation and allergic reactions can occur. It must be kept away from the eyes and ears, where it can cause eye damage or inner-ear toxicity.

angle.text: Hibiclens, a hospital chlorhexidine antiseptic wash, is used on underarms to cut the bacteria behind odor. Its antibacterial action is well established; odor outcomes have not been studied.

lead: Hibiclens is a brand of topical chlorhexidine skin cleanser, one of several chlorhexidine brands.[1] Chlorhexidine is an antiseptic used to prepare skin before surgery, clean wounds and in surgical scrubs, and is sold over the counter in the US.[1] In looksmaxxing and body-care discussions it is used as a body wash for underarm odor, on the idea that it reduces odor-causing skin bacteria.

In hospitals, daily bathing of intensive care patients with chlorhexidine-soaked washcloths reduced hospital-acquired infections in one US trial.[1] Studies of chlorhexidine for cosmetic body odor were not found.
infobox: OTC in US; WHO essential medicines list[1]

paras: Chlorhexidine releases a positively charged molecule that binds bacterial cell walls. At low concentrations it halts bacterial multiplication, and at higher concentrations it disrupts the membrane and kills them. It does not destroy bacterial spores.[1]

Proponents say killing underarm bacteria stops them converting sweat into odor. The body odor article says daily bathing with antibacterial soap lowers the skin's bacterial load, and that odor arises from bacterial breakdown of apocrine sweat.[2]

Reported effects include skin irritation, allergic reactions and tooth staining; eye contact can cause problems, and it is toxic to the inner ear if it enters the middle ear through a ruptured eardrum.[1] Analyses spanning decades found no change in chlorhexidine's effectiveness against surgical site infection organisms.[1]

Separately, the FDA's 2016 final rule prohibited 19 active ingredients in over-the-counter consumer antibacterial washes, citing inadequate evidence of benefit beyond plain soap; the rule did not cover healthcare settings.[3] Chlorhexidine was not among the ingredients described in the reference text reviewed.

No studies found for body odor. Research on handwashing with plain soap in community settings found reductions in gastrointestinal illness of about 31 percent in a meta-analysis of hand-hygiene interventions, which concerns infection prevention rather than odor.[4]
